title: The Single-Cell Pediatric Cancer Atlas: Data portal and open-source tools for single-cell transcriptomics of pediatric tumors
abstract: The Single-Cell Pediatric Cancer Atlas (ScPCA) Portal is a resource for uniformly processed single-cell and single-nucleus RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) data and de-identified metadata from pediatric tumor samples. Originally comprising data from 10 projects funded by Alex's Lemonade Stand Foundation (ALSF), the Portal currently contains summarized gene expression data for over 700 samples across 55 cancer types from ALSF-funded and community-contributed datasets. Downloads include expression data as SingleCellExperiment or AnnData objects containing raw and normalized counts, principal-component analysis (PCA) and uniform manifold approximation and projection (UMAP) coordinates, automated cell-type annotations, and copy-number variation estimates, along with summary reports. Some samples have additional data from bulk RNA-seq, spatial transcriptomics, and/or feature barcoding (e.g., CITE-seq) included in the download. All data on the Portal were uniformly processed using scpca-nf, an efficient and open-source Nextflow workflow that uses alevin-fry to quantify gene expression. Comprehensive documentation, including file descriptions and a getting-started guide, are available online.

summary.tldr: The Single-Cell Pediatric Cancer Atlas is a new data portal providing uniformly processed single-cell RNA sequencing data and tools for studying childhood tumors.
summary.problem: Researchers need a centralized and uniformly processed collection of single-cell and single-nucleus RNA sequencing data specifically focused on pediatric cancers.
summary.methods: The authors developed a data portal that aggregates over 700 pediatric tumor samples across 55 cancer types, processing all data uniformly with an open-source Nextflow workflow called scpca-nf.
summary.findings: The portal offers downloadable data objects that include raw and normalized gene counts, cell-type annotations, and dimensionality reduction coordinates, with some samples also featuring spatial transcriptomics or bulk RNA sequencing data.
summary.why: Providing standardized and ready-to-use datasets alongside comprehensive documentation makes it much easier for researchers to analyze pediatric cancer data without having to process raw files from scratch.
summary.limitations: The provided text does not mention any specific limitations of the portal or the data.
summary.takeaway: The ScPCA Portal provides the research community with a large, uniformly processed, and easily accessible collection of single-cell data for pediatric tumors.

title: A complete diploid human genome benchmark for personalized genomics
abstract: Human genome resequencing typically involves mapping reads to a reference genome to call variants; however, this approach suffers from both technical and reference biases, leaving many duplicated and structurally polymorphic regions of the genome unmapped. Consequently, existing variant benchmarks, generated by the same methods, fail to assess these complex regions. To address this limitation, we present a telomere-to-telomere genome benchmark that achieves near-perfect accuracy (i.e. no detectable errors) across 99.4% of the complete, diploid HG002 genome. This benchmark adds 701.4 Mb of autosomal sequence and both sex chromosomes (216.8 Mb), totaling 15.3% of the genome that was absent from prior benchmarks. We also provide a diploid annotation of genes, transposable elements, segmental duplications, and satellite repeats, including 39,144 protein-coding genes across both haplotypes. To facilitate application of the benchmark, we developed tools for measuring the accuracy of sequencing reads, phased variant call sets, and genome assemblies against a diploid reference. Genome-wide analyses show that state-of-the-art de novo assembly methods resolve 2-7% more sequence and outperform variant calling accuracy by an order of magnitude, yielding just one error per 100 kb across 99.9% of the benchmark regions. Adoption of genome-based benchmarking is expected to accelerate the development of cost-effective methods for complete genome sequencing, expanding the reach of genomic medicine to the entire genome and enabling a new era of personalized genomics.

summary.tldr: Researchers created a highly accurate complete diploid human genome benchmark that includes previously unmapped complex regions along with tools to evaluate sequencing and assembly methods.
summary.problem: Standard genome sequencing methods map reads to a reference which creates biases and leaves complex duplicated or structurally variable regions unmapped meaning existing benchmarks miss these difficult areas.
summary.methods: The authors developed a telomere-to-telomere benchmark for the complete diploid HG002 genome annotated its features across both sets of chromosomes and created new software tools to measure the accuracy of sequencing reads variant calls and genome assemblies.
summary.findings: The new benchmark covers 99.4 percent of the genome with near-perfect accuracy adding over 900 megabases of sequence that older benchmarks missed. Using this benchmark they found that modern de novo assembly methods map 2 to 7 percent more sequence and are significantly more accurate at identifying variants than traditional read-mapping techniques.
summary.why: A complete and accurate benchmark allows scientists to evaluate and improve sequencing technologies which will help make whole-genome sequencing more cost-effective and comprehensive for personalized medicine.
summary.limitations: The provided text does not explicitly mention any limitations of the study.
summary.takeaway: A new nearly flawless benchmark for the complete human genome reveals that de novo assembly is vastly superior to traditional variant calling paving the way for better personalized genomic medicine.

verifier_notes: The summary is largely faithful but slightly overstates/rephrases the added sequence figure; the 918 Mb sum is defensible, making this borderline, but 'map' vs 'resolve' is a minor distortion.

title: igraph 1.0 enables fast and robust network analysis across programming languages
abstract: Networks or graphs are widely used across the sciences to represent relationships of many kinds. The igraph (https://igraph.org) software library supports graph construction, analysis, and visualisation, combining fast and robust performance with a low entry barrier. igraph pairs a fast core written in C with beginner-friendly interfaces in Python, R, and Mathematica. After twenty years of development, igraph 1.0 has been released, enabling public access to a robust and stable network analysis with over a million monthly downloads. Thanks to its cross-language design, igraph delivers both speed and flexibility: it can handle billions of edges, supports interactive plotting, integrates with notebooks, facilitates conversions to and from other network libraries, includes a rich library of graph layout and community detection algorithms, and has a detailed documentation including non-English translations. Modern testing features such as continuous integration, address sanitizers, stricter typing, and memory-managed vectors have also increased robustness. Hundreds of bug reports have been fixed and a community forum has been opened to connect users and developers. Specific effort has been made to broaden use and community participation by women, non-binary people, and other demographic groups typically underrepresented in open source software.

summary.tldr: The release of igraph 1.0 provides a fast, robust, and accessible cross-language software library for network analysis and visualization.
summary.problem: Researchers need a fast, reliable, and easy-to-use tool to construct, analyze, and visualize complex networks across different programming languages.
summary.methods: The developers built a core library in C for speed and created user-friendly interfaces for Python, R, and Mathematica, while implementing modern software testing techniques like continuous integration and memory management to ensure stability.
summary.findings: After twenty years of development, igraph 1.0 successfully handles billions of edges, offers extensive algorithms for layout and community detection, integrates well with other tools, and has achieved over a million monthly downloads with improved stability and community support.
summary.why: It provides a highly efficient and flexible foundational tool for scientists across various disciplines to analyze massive network datasets without needing advanced programming expertise.
summary.limitations: The provided text does not mention any specific limitations of the software.
summary.takeaway: igraph 1.0 is a mature, high-performance, and inclusive open-source library that makes large-scale network analysis accessible across multiple popular programming languages.

title: Comprehensive benchmarking of tools for nanopore-based detection of DNA methylation
abstract: Oxford Nanopore (ONT) sequencing offers direct detection of DNA base modifications. Numerous tools have been developed to leverage this advantage. However, their performance remains unclear. Here, using diverse bacterial, plant, and mammalian datasets, we systematically evaluate the current landscape of nanopore methylation tools. We demonstrate that although most recent tools perform well, older models remain the reliable choice for studying CpG methylation. Conversely, newer models show substantial improvement in identifying 5-methylcytosine in non-CpG contexts, 6-methyladenine, and 4-methylcytosine. Further, we highlight the sensitivity of tools to confounding methylation nearby, assess their computational performance, and evaluate the effects of sequencing depth, methylation abundance, read quality, and basecalling mode. We provide reusable pipelines and open access datasets to empower future benchmarking efforts. Our work thus details the strengths and limitations of the state-of-the-art methylation models and outlines practical guidelines for researchers using nanopore sequencing to study DNA methylation.

summary.tldr: This study evaluates various software tools for detecting different types of DNA methylation using the latest Oxford Nanopore sequencing technology, providing guidelines on which tools work best for specific modifications.
summary.problem: While Oxford Nanopore sequencing can directly detect DNA modifications, it is unclear how well current software tools perform on the latest sequencing chemistry, especially for modifications outside of the standard mammalian CpG context, such as non-CpG 5mC, 6mA, and 4mC.
summary.methods: Researchers sequenced DNA from bacteria, plants, mice, and humans using the latest nanopore technology. They compared the methylation calls from several software tools, including Dorado, DeepBAM, DeepMod2, DeepPlant, f5C, and RockFish, against highly accurate ground-truth data generated via chemical conversion methods and PacBio sequencing. They assessed accuracy, computational speed, memory usage, and the impact of neighboring modifications and read quality.
summary.findings: The study found that older models like Dorado v4r1 and RockFish remain the most accurate for detecting standard CpG methylation. However, newer models like Dorado v5r3 are much better at identifying non-CpG methylation, 6mA, and 4mC. The tools varied widely in speed and memory usage, and many struggled with accuracy when other methylated bases were nearby. The authors also found that filtering for high-quality reads and having at least 20x sequencing coverage significantly improved results.
summary.why: By detailing the strengths and weaknesses of current software, this research helps scientists choose the most appropriate and efficient tools for their specific DNA methylation studies, ultimately improving the reliability of epigenetic research.
summary.limitations: The chemical conversion method used as the ground truth can introduce its own biases. Additionally, the study did not evaluate 5-hydroxymethylcytosine, was limited in its analysis of the rare 4mC modification, and had to rely on a database rather than direct sequencing data for two of the bacterial samples.
summary.takeaway: No single software tool is perfect for all types of DNA methylation; researchers should use older models for standard CpG sites and newer models for other modifications, while ensuring high sequencing coverage and read quality.

title: Tropical Geometry of Phylogenetic Tree Space: A statistical Perspective
abstract: Abstract Phylogenetic trees are the fundamental mathematical representation of evolutionary processes in biology. They are also objects of interest in pure mathematics, such as algebraic geometry and combinatorics, due to their discrete geometry. Although they are important data structures, they face the significant challenge that sets of trees form a non-Euclidean phylogenetic tree space, which means that standard computational and statistical methods cannot be directly applied. In this work, we explore the statistical feasibility of a pure mathematical representation of the set of all phylogenetic trees based on tropical geometry for both descriptive and inferential statistics, and unsupervised and supervised machine learning. Our exploration is both theoretical and practical. We show that the tropical geometric phylogenetic tree space endowed with a generalized Hilbert projective metric exhibits analytic, geometric, and topological properties that are desirable for theoretical studies in probability and statistics and allow for well-defined questions to be posed. We illustrate the statistical feasibility of the tropical geometric perspective for phylogenetic trees with an example of both a descriptive and inferential statistical task. Moreover, this approach exhibits increased computational efficiency and statistical performance over the current state-of-the-art, which we illustrate with a real data example on seasonal influenza. Our results demonstrate the viability of the tropical geometric setting for parametric statistical and probabilistic studies of sets of phylogenetic trees.

summary.tldr: This paper introduces a tropical geometry framework for analyzing sets of phylogenetic trees, offering a more computationally efficient and statistically robust alternative to traditional non-Euclidean tree spaces.
summary.problem: Standard statistical and machine learning methods cannot be directly applied to sets of phylogenetic trees because they form a complex, non-Euclidean geometric space where averages tend to stick to lower dimensions and data visualization is mathematically restricted.
summary.methods: The researchers modeled phylogenetic trees using tropical geometry, creating a metric space called palm tree space. They mathematically proved this space supports rigorous probability and statistics, then developed tropical versions of Principal Component Analysis and Linear Discriminant Analysis, testing them on simulated data and real seasonal influenza virus genomes.
summary.findings: Palm tree space satisfies the mathematical requirements for rigorous statistical analysis and allows for faster computation of distances between trees compared to the standard approach. In real-world tests, tropical PCA captured more of the data variance and revealed richer evolutionary structures in influenza viruses, while tropical LDA accurately classified simulated evolutionary trees.
summary.why: It provides biologists and statisticians with a practical, mathematically sound toolkit to perform exact statistical inference and machine learning on complex evolutionary datasets, which is crucial for tracking pathogen spread and understanding evolutionary history.
summary.limitations: The shortest path between two trees in this tropical space is generally not unique, which means the statistical average of a set of trees is also not unique, potentially complicating some analyses.
summary.takeaway: Representing phylogenetic trees through tropical geometry overcomes major statistical hurdles of traditional tree spaces, enabling faster and more accurate machine learning and statistical analysis on evolutionary data.

title: Inferring variant-specific effective reproduction numbers from combined case and sequencing data
abstract: Accurately estimating relative transmission rates of SARS-CoV-2 variants remains a scientific and public health priority. Recent studies have used the sample proportions of different variants from genetic sequence data to describe variant frequency dynamics and relative transmission rates, but frequencies alone cannot capture the rich epidemiological behavior of SARS-CoV-2. Here, we extend methods for inferring the effective reproduction number of an epidemic using confirmed case data to jointly estimate variant-specific effective reproduction numbers and frequencies of co-circulating variants using cases and sequences across states in the United States from January 2021 to March 2022. Our method can be used to infer structured relationships between effective reproduction numbers across time series, allowing us to estimate fixed variant-specific growth advantages. We use this model to estimate the effective reproduction number of SARS-CoV-2 variants of concern and variants of interest in the United States, and to estimate consistent growth advantages of particular variants across different locations.

summary.tldr: Researchers developed a new method that combines case counts and genetic sequencing data to accurately estimate the transmission rates and growth advantages of different SARS-CoV-2 variants.
summary.problem: Previous methods relied only on the frequency of different variants in genetic sequences to estimate transmission rates, which fails to capture the full epidemiological complexity of how the virus spreads.
summary.methods: The authors expanded existing epidemic modeling techniques by combining confirmed case data with genetic sequencing data from the United States between January 2021 and March 2022 to jointly calculate variant frequencies and their specific reproduction numbers.
summary.findings: The new model successfully estimated the effective reproduction numbers for various SARS-CoV-2 variants of concern and interest, revealing consistent growth advantages for specific variants across different geographic locations.
summary.why: Accurately measuring how fast different viral variants spread is crucial for public health planning and understanding the dynamics of an ongoing pandemic.
summary.limitations: The provided text does not mention any specific limitations of the study.
summary.takeaway: Combining overall case counts with genetic sequencing data provides a more accurate and detailed picture of how specific viral variants spread and outcompete others.

title: Accelerating scientific discovery with Co-Scientist
abstract: Abstract Scientific discovery is driven by scientists generating hypotheses for complex problems that undergo rigorous experimental validation. To augment this process, we introduce Co-Scientist, a multi-agent artificial intelligence (AI) system built on Gemini for structured scientific thinking and hypothesis generation. Co-Scientist aims to help scientists discover new original knowledge. Conditioned on their research objectives and previous scientific evidence, it formulates demonstrably novel research hypotheses for experimental verification. The system’s design involves agents continuously generating, critiquing and refining hypotheses accelerated by scaling test-time compute. Key contributions include (1) a multi-agent architecture with an asynchronous task execution framework for flexible compute scaling, and (2) a tournament evolution process for self-improving hypotheses generation. Automated evaluations show continued benefits of test-time compute scaling, improving hypothesis quality over time. Although this is a general-purpose system, we focus the validation in three biomedical applications: drug repurposing; novel-target discovery 1 ; and explaining mechanisms of antimicrobial resistance 2 . Specifically, Co-Scientist helped to identify new drug-repurposing candidates and synergistic combination therapies for acute myeloid leukaemia that were validated through in vitro experiments. These real-world validations demonstrate the potential of Co-Scientist to accelerate scientific discovery and usher in an era of AI-empowered scientists.

summary.tldr: Researchers developed Co-Scientist, a multi-agent AI system that accelerates scientific discovery by autonomously generating, debating, and refining novel research hypotheses.
summary.problem: The rapid expansion of scientific literature makes it difficult for researchers to maintain both the deep specialized expertise and broad interdisciplinary knowledge needed to generate novel scientific hypotheses.
summary.methods: The team built a multi-agent AI system powered by large language models that mimics the scientific method through specialized agents designed to generate, critique, rank, and evolve ideas. The system was tested on complex biomedical problems, and its top AI-generated hypotheses for acute myeloid leukemia drug repurposing were validated using in vitro laboratory experiments on human cancer cell lines.
summary.findings: The AI system successfully proposed novel, experimentally valid hypotheses, including identifying new single-drug and combination therapies for acute myeloid leukemia that effectively killed cancer cells in the lab. It also successfully identified new treatment targets for liver fibrosis and accurately deduced a complex, unpublished mechanism behind bacterial antimicrobial resistance.
summary.why: By acting as an intelligent collaborator that can synthesize vast amounts of literature and reason across disciplines, this AI tool can significantly speed up the early stages of research and uncover therapeutic candidates that human experts might miss.
summary.limitations: The system is limited by its reliance on open-access literature, meaning it may miss paywalled research or unpublished negative results, and it is still susceptible to AI hallucinations, requiring rigorous human oversight and further real-world clinical validation.
summary.takeaway: Multi-agent AI systems can effectively augment human scientists by iteratively generating and refining testable research hypotheses, demonstrating real-world utility in fields like drug discovery and molecular biology.

title: IQ-TREE 3: phylogenomic inference software using complex evolutionary models
abstract: IQ-TREE (https://iqtree.github.io/) is a widely used open-source software tool for efficiently inferring phylogenetic trees under maximum likelihood. Here, we present IQ-TREE version 3, the third major release of the software. IQ-TREE 3 significantly extends version 2 with new features, including mixture models as an alternative to partitioned models, gene and site concordance factors to quantify discordance between genomic regions, integration with phylogenomic divergence time estimation, and a fully featured sequence simulator. The IQ-TREE 3 source code is available at https://github.com/iqtree/iqtree3.

summary.tldr: IQ-TREE 3 is a major update to a popular phylogenetic software tool, introducing advanced evolutionary models, sequence simulation, and tools for analyzing massive datasets like pandemic viral genomes.
summary.problem: Researchers need robust, efficient software to accurately reconstruct evolutionary trees from increasingly large and complex genomic datasets, while accounting for varying evolutionary processes across different genes and sites.
summary.methods: The developers updated the IQ-TREE software to version 3 by integrating several new algorithms and models. These include automatic mixture models for DNA and proteins, concordance factors to measure evolutionary discordance, a built-in sequence simulator called AliSim, new clade-specific protein models, tools for pandemic-scale datasets, and workflows for estimating divergence times.
summary.findings: IQ-TREE 3 successfully incorporates these new features, allowing users to automatically apply complex mixture models without manual data partitioning, simulate sequences faster than older tools, root trees without outgroups using nonreversible models, and analyze millions of closely related sequences efficiently.
summary.why: Accurate evolutionary trees are fundamental to understanding biology, biodiversity, and the spread of pathogens. By providing more realistic models and handling massive datasets, IQ-TREE 3 helps scientists avoid common errors in tree-building and track disease outbreaks more effectively.
summary.limitations: The authors note that using mixture models requires more computational time and memory compared to simpler models. Additionally, the new MAST model requires users to manually provide a set of input tree topologies to test.
summary.takeaway: IQ-TREE 3 offers a powerful, comprehensive suite of tools for modern evolutionary analysis, making it easier for researchers to apply complex models to both deep evolutionary questions and rapid pathogen tracking.

title: BioMaster: Multi-agent system for automated bioinformatics analysis workflow
abstract: Abstract Motivation The rapid expansion of biological data has significantly increased the complexity of bioinformatics workflows, which often involve intricate, multi-step processes. These tasks demand considerable manual effort from bioinformaticians, creating inefficiencies and limiting scalability. Recent advancements in large language model (LLM)-powered agents offer promising solutions to streamline and automate these workflows. However, existing automated systems, while effective for short, well-defined tasks, often struggle with long, multi-step workflows due to challenges such as error propagation, limited adaptability to emerging tools, and the inability of LLMs to generalize to niche bioinformatics tasks. Achieving effective workflow automation requires robust task coordination, dynamic knowledge retrieval, and mechanisms to ensure errors are identified and resolved before they impact downstream processes. Results We present BioMaster, a multi-agent framework designed to automate and streamline complex bioinformatics workflows. BioMaster incorporates specialized agents with role-based responsibilities, enabling precise task decomposition, execution, and validation. It leverages Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) to dynamically retrieve domain-specific knowledge, improving adaptability to new tools and niche analyses. BioMaster also introduces enhanced control over input and output validation to ensure pipeline consistency and employs a memory management strategy optimized for handling long workflows. Experiments across diverse bioinformatics tasks, including RNA-seq, ChIP-seq, single-cell analysis, and Hi-C processing, demonstrate that BioMaster significantly outperforms existing methods in accuracy, efficiency, and scalability. By addressing key limitations in workflow automation, BioMaster offers a robust solution for modern bioinformatics challenges. Availability https://github.com/ai4nucleome/BioMaster Contact yanlinzhang@hkust-gz.edu.cn

summary.tldr: BioMaster is a new multi-agent artificial intelligence system designed to automate complex, multi-step bioinformatics workflows with high accuracy and efficiency.
summary.problem: As biological data grows, analyzing it requires complex, multi-step workflows that demand significant manual effort. While large language models can help, current automated systems struggle with long workflows because errors pile up, they cannot easily adapt to new tools, and they fail at highly specialized tasks.
summary.methods: The researchers developed BioMaster, a framework using multiple specialized AI agents that divide, execute, and check tasks. The system uses Retrieval-Augmented Generation to pull in specific biological knowledge as needed, includes strict checks on data moving between steps, and features a memory system built specifically for long processes.
summary.findings: When tested on various tasks like RNA sequencing, single-cell analysis, and Hi-C processing, BioMaster was significantly more accurate, efficient, and scalable than existing automated methods.
summary.why: Automating these complex pipelines reduces the manual burden on researchers, speeds up data analysis, and makes it easier to handle the massive amounts of data generated in modern biology.
summary.limitations: The provided text does not mention any specific limitations of the system or the study.
summary.takeaway: By using specialized AI agents and dynamic knowledge retrieval, BioMaster successfully automates long and complex bioinformatics analyses, outperforming current tools.

title: Advancing bioinformatics with language models: components, applications, and perspectives
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are a class of artificial intelligence models based on deep learning, which have great performance in various tasks, especially in natural language processing (NLP). Large language models typically consist of artificial neural networks with numerous parameters, trained on large amounts of unlabeled input using self-supervised or semi-supervised learning. However, their potential for solving bioinformatics problems may even exceed their proficiency in modeling human language. In this review, we will provide a comprehensive overview of the essential components of large language models (LLMs) in bioinformatics, spanning genomics, transcriptomics, proteomics, drug discovery, and single-cell analysis. Key aspects covered include tokenization methods for diverse data types, the architecture of transformer models, the core attention mechanism, and the pre-training processes underlying these models. Additionally, we will introduce currently available foundation models and highlight their downstream applications across various bioinformatics domains. Finally, drawing from our experience, we will offer practical guidance for both LLM users and developers, emphasizing strategies to optimize their use and foster further innovation in the field.

summary.tldr: This review provides a comprehensive overview of how large language models are built and applied across various fields of bioinformatics.
summary.problem: Researchers need a structured understanding of how large language models, originally designed for human text, can be adapted to solve complex biological problems.
summary.methods: The authors reviewed the essential components of large language models in bioinformatics, including tokenization, transformer architectures, attention mechanisms, pre-training processes, and existing foundation models.
summary.findings: The review details how large language models are being successfully applied across genomics, transcriptomics, proteomics, drug discovery, and single-cell analysis, suggesting their potential in biology may exceed their success in human language.
summary.why: Understanding the underlying mechanics and current applications of these models helps researchers optimize their use and fosters further innovation in biological data analysis.
summary.limitations: The provided text does not mention any specific limitations of the review or the models discussed.
summary.takeaway: Large language models are powerful tools for bioinformatics, and understanding their core components is essential for developing new applications in the field.
